analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top federal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25%.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the corporate tax rate from 35% to 25% was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on February 10, 2011, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lower the top federal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25% on income above $50,000, with a temporary 30% rate on income above $75,000 for 2011 as a transition. The cut would go to corporations, whose savings flow mainly to shareholders — households that own most corporate stock. It was introduced by Rep. Richard Hanna with 32 Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a hearing or a vote [S1] [S4] [S5] [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations with income above $50,000, and the shareholders who receive their after-tax profits. Corporate stock is held disproportionately by wealthier households, so the bulk of the tax savings would flow to them. Companies with income between $50,000 and $75,000 would also see their rate drop from 25% to 15% under the bill's structure [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the maximum corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25% on taxable income exceeding $50,000, applying to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2010 [S3] [S2].
For the 2011 transition year, sets a maximum 30% rate on corporate income above $75,000, keeping the first-year rate higher than the permanent rate the bill would set afterward [S3] [S2].
Conforms related Code provisions — such as the rates used for certain refunds, foreign tax credit, and recapture rules — to the new maximum rate, replacing references to the 35% rate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The corporate income tax is the main direct tax on corporate profits; cutting it reduces federal revenue, which must be made up by borrowing, by higher taxes elsewhere, or by cutting federal spending. The savings from the rate cut themselves concentrate among shareholders, who are disproportionately higher-income households.

drawbacks.text: The bill reduces federal revenue with no offset, so the shortfall would add to deficits or force other taxes or spending to fill the gap — costs that fall on the general public [S3].

The direct benefits concentrate among shareholders. Corporate stock ownership is skewed toward higher-income households, so a broad corporate rate cut delivers most of its value to them rather than to working taxpayers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose is to improve business competitiveness by lowering the corporate rate from 35% to 25% [S3]. The cost is a broad reduction in federal revenue with no identified replacement, and the direct gains go to corporations and their shareholders rather than to most working households. The 2011-only 30% rate on income above $75,000 modestly limits the first-year revenue loss but does not change the long-term picture [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and it stayed there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Hanna (R-NY) introduced the bill on February 10, 2011, with 16 original cosponsors joining the introduction [S3] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day and never advanced beyond that referral — no committee vote, no report, no floor action appears in its history [S5] [S1].
The bill attracted 32 cosponsors in total, all Republicans, but that support never translated into committee action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the corporate rate stayed at 35% for the rest of the 112th Congress. Federal revenue was not cut, and the public did not bear the cost of the tax reduction. Corporations and shareholders, who would have been the bill's direct beneficiaries, are worse off than they would have been had it passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General federal taxpayers; the rate cut never happened

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democratic cosponsors appear in the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have cut the rate applied to corporate income above $50,000 from 35% to 25%, a direct reduction in what profitable corporations owe the federal government. Because it never passed, their tax rate remained 35% through 2012.

industries.industry: Small and mid-sized corporations with income near $50,000
industries.note: The bill keeps the 15% rate on income up to $50,000 unchanged, so the smallest corporations are unaffected; those earning between $50,000 and $75,000 would gain the most proportionally, moving from a 25% to a 15% rate on that band.

Corporate tax savings ultimately flow to shareholders through higher after-tax profits, and stock ownership is concentrated among wealthier households, so this group would have captured most of the rate cut's value.
